addressed_problems.content: Current dataset distillation methods (e.g., Efficient Dataset Condensation) achieve limited accuracy on harder datasets and do not generalize well across architectures: on CIFAR-10, distilled datasets with 10 images per class yield 50.6–74.5% accuracy depending on compression, and performance on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K is significantly lower. Consequently, distilled pruning cannot yet serve as a standalone replacement for iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) when final test performance is the priority. It remains an open question how to improve distillation quality and cross-architecture generalization so that distilled pruning can match or exceed IMP performance at high sparsities on standard benchmarks.

The authors show that distilled pruning removes parameters that correlate with reduced sharpness of the loss landscape, as evidenced by tighter Hessian diagonal distributions, lower loss barriers in linear mode connectivity, and flatter basins in loss-landscape visualizations. However, a deeper theoretical understanding or layer-wise analytical account of why these parameters are removed—and how the compression of distilled data mechanistically selects for landscape smoothness—is not provided. This leaves an unresolved gap: the causal link between distilled-data-driven parameter selection and the resulting stability properties of the subnetwork.

Analysis of sparsity masks from distilled pruning and traditional IMP revealed no clear structural patterns; the masks are nearly independent in the distribution of zeros and have similar per-layer sparsity and weight-magnitude distributions. It remains an open empirical question which microcharacteristics of pruned parameters (e.g., their functional role, connectivity patterns, or feature selectivity) determine whether distilled pruning or IMP will select them. Further investigation into these microcharacteristics could inform the design of more principled pruning algorithms.

Current distilled pruning is limited to small datasets (CIFAR, MNIST) due to the high computational cost of optimizing synthetic training sets and the under-performance of distillation on ImageNet-1K. The authors suggest that improved distillation algorithms or alternative synthetic-data construction strategies (e.g., knowledge distillation from the dense model) may be essential for scaling to larger architectures and datasets. It remains unresolved whether such advances can enable distilled pruning to find stable lottery tickets—sparse trainable subnetworks at initialization—in real-world large-scale settings, such as full ImageNet-1K or large-scale vision and language models.

Distilled pruning increases the stability of subnetworks at initialization, as measured by linear mode connectivity and Hessian analysis, but this stability can come at the cost of reduced final accuracy when the distilled data is poorly aligned with the training set (e.g., on CIFAR-100). The trade-off between increased stability and occasional loss in performance is not yet algorithmically resolved. Methods that preserve both high distilled-data compression (i.e., fewer images per class) and high downstream accuracy remain an open research objective.

Sparse neural network training and pruning face a practical and theoretical bottleneck: while iterative pruning methods such as Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with weight rewinding can empirically locate sparse initializations that can be trained to match dense performance (the "lottery ticket" phenomenon), these procedures are computationally expensive because they repeatedly train networks to convergence and rely on post-training information to decide which parameters to prune. More fundamentally, prior work has shown that finding high-performing sparse initializations by rewinding to the random initialization only succeeds when the dense initialization is "stable" to SGD noise (training under different data orderings leads to models that are linearly mode connected). Larger models and realistic datasets are typically unstable at initialization, so the brute-force IMP procedure either fails to find lottery tickets or must instead rewind to an early point in training (yielding "matching subnetworks" rather than true lottery tickets). Separately, dataset distillation methods compress a real training set into a tiny synthetic set optimized to reproduce training trajectories, offering dramatic reductions in data used per training run. However, dataset distillation is currently limited: it is computationally expensive to optimize, tends to over-compress and lose image-specific information on harder datasets, generalizes poorly across architectures, and its implications for pruning dynamics and stability are unexplored. Consequently, there is a missing capability in the literature: an efficient, principled mechanism to (a) use far fewer training points to evaluate parameter importance for pruning at initialization, (b) understand whether using compressed synthetic data changes the stability properties of subnetworks discovered at initialization, and (c) leverage any such changes to extend the practical reach of lottery-ticket-style sparse initializations to larger models or higher sparsities. This gap prevents both efficient pruning at initialization for realistic settings and a theoretical/empirical understanding of how the choice of data used during pruning affects the loss landscape, stability to SGD noise, and the existence of trainable sparse subnetworks.

nodes.content: In order to find sparse initializations that can be trained in isolation (true lottery tickets) practitioners typically use Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with full training on the real dataset in each pruning iteration; this is costly because each pruning iteration requires training to convergence on the full dataset. Dataset distillation offers a route to dramatically shrink the inner-loop training set, but prior to this work there was no established algorithmic procedure showing how to integrate distilled data into iterative pruning while preserving the semantics of weight-rewinding and mask selection. Researchers needed a concrete, operational method that defines how to run pruning iterations on synthetic data, how to prune and rewind in that setting, and how to interpret the resulting mask when training on real data. Without such a method, there was no validated protocol to exploit synthetic data to reduce computation during mask discovery or to study how compressed data influences which parameters are deemed important.

The community has observed that the existence of lottery tickets from random initialization is tied to stability of the dense initialization: when the dense model is stable to SGD noise (models trained with different data orderings converge to linearly connected minima), IMP can find masks that correspond to lottery tickets; when instability exists, IMP's mask selection becomes unreliable because retraining can land in different minima and invalidate post-training mask decisions. Prior remedies have included rewinding to an early point in training (producing matching subnetworks rather than true lottery tickets) or applying weight permutation techniques. Before this work it was not known whether changing the dataset used during the pruning inner loop—specifically, substituting distilled synthetic data—could produce sparsity masks that are intrinsically more stable at initialization than those produced by standard IMP, thereby enabling true sparse training from random initialization even when the dense initialization is unstable. Establishing whether stability can be obtained at initialization without changing the initialization itself (i.e., by changing the data used to select the mask) is essential to extend lottery-ticket-style results to broader settings without having to adopt rewinding or permutation interventions.

If pruning at initialization removes parameters that influence landscape sharpness, then masks selected using different data could change whether retraining lands in the same minima or in different minima, thereby affecting the utility of masks discovered by IMP. Prior to this work, there was limited empirical evidence connecting the data used for mask discovery to explicit measures of loss sharpness or to two-dimensional visualizations of the landscape around trained solutions. Researchers therefore lacked measurements that tie a change in pruning-data modality (real vs. distilled) to concrete geometric and curvature properties of the loss landscape that determine stability and retrainability of sparse initializations. Without such measurements, it remained unclear whether distilled-data-based mask selection mechanistically reduces sharpness and thereby increases stability.

Vanilla IMP applied to an unstable dense initialization fails to find lottery tickets at high sparsities because retraining after pruning can move the sparse model into different minima, invalidating mask choices made with post-training weight information. Existing work solves this by rewinding to an early training point (yielding matching subnetworks) or by other interventions, but those remedies either disqualify the initialization as a true lottery ticket or add extra training cost. There was no validated approach that exploits a computationally cheap preprocessing step to transform an unstable dense initialization into a stable sparse initialization from which standard IMP can successfully discover true lottery tickets at higher sparsities. A method that achieves this would extend the set of initializations where true sparse training from initialization is possible without requiring costly retraining or abandoning the "from-initialization" requirement.

The promise of dataset distillation is to replace or heavily shrink the real inner-loop training set when optimizing models or model-selection procedures, but existing distillation methods do not uniformly preserve downstream task performance across datasets and architectures: they often over-compress and lose task-relevant signal on harder datasets and generalize poorly across architectures. Therefore, it was unknown whether substituting distilled data in the inner loop of an expensive pruning protocol could both reduce computational cost and preserve the final sparse-model performance; if not, the value of distilled pruning would be limited. Practitioners needed empirical quantification of the performance-versus-compression trade-off to know when distilled pruning is a viable computational shortcut versus when it is a destabilizing approximation that degrades final accuracy.

Understanding whether different pruning-data modalities select the same or different parameters is essential to interpret why distilled pruning changes stability and landscape sharpness. If distilled pruning simply reorders the same set of pruned weights as IMP, then differences in stability would demand a different explanation; conversely, if the masks are structurally different, that supports a mechanistic account where distilled pruning removes parameters contributing to sharpness. Prior to this work there was no empirical comparison of mask overlap and per-weight magnitude statistics between masks produced by trajectory-matching distilled-data pruning and masks produced by standard IMP from the same initialization, leaving a gap in mechanistic understanding of how the choice of pruning data modality affects which parameters are considered important.

Distilled Pruning is an operational procedure that replaces the real-data inner-loop training of Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with training on a small synthetic dataset produced by a dataset distillation method that matches training trajectories. Concretely, the algorithm iteratively: (i) trains the network to convergence on a distilled synthetic set (e.g., 1–50 images per class), (ii) prunes the lowest-magnitude 20% of weights by magnitude, (iii) rewinds the remaining weights to their original random initialization, and (iv) repeats until the target sparsity mask is obtained. The resulting sparsity mask applied to the original initialization defines a "synthetic subnetwork" that can subsequently be trained on the real dataset. This procedure reduces the number of real training points used to select a sparsity mask by orders of magnitude relative to standard IMP and produces sparse subnetworks at initialization.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that distilled pruning produces sparse subnetworks at initialization is operationally defined and validated on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 (H1). However, a load-bearing uncertainty (P1) remains: the procedure's reliance on synthetic training to rank weight importance correctly is not independently verified, threatening the claim's generality beyond the tested configuration. P1 and H1 are partially offsetting—H1 demonstrates success in one case but does not establish the assumption across all cases. The conclusion's credibility is moderate and heavily scoped to the specific setting where it has been tested.

nodes.title: Distilled Pruning: iterative magnitude pruning using dataset-distilled data to produce synthetic subnetworks

nodes.content: Sparse subnetworks discovered by Distilled Pruning ("synthetic subnetworks") often train to solutions that are linearly mode connected across different shufflings of the real training data, i.e., they exhibit low or zero loss barriers under linear interpolation between weights trained on different data orders. Empirically, for studied settings (e.g., ConvNet-3 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-10 on ImageNet-10) the dense initialization is unstable (trained models land in different minima), yet the synthetic subnetworks obtained by pruning on distilled data are stable to SGD noise at initialization: interpolating between two independently trained versions of the same synthetic subnetwork shows little or no increase in training loss, indicating linear mode connectivity for the sparse initialization.

metadata.narrative: The stability of synthetic subnetworks at initialization is supported by replicated linear mode connectivity experiments on ConvNet-3/CIFAR-10 and ResNet-10/ImageNet-10 (H2). However, the generalization to larger models and full-scale datasets is untested (P2). P2 acts as a scope restrictor: the conclusion holds in the demonstrated regimes but should not be assumed beyond them. The primary risk is that the conclusion's broader significance (advancing lottery tickets to realistic settings) depends on scaling, which is not validated. The narrative operates on B (P2 is a show-stopper for large-scale claims) and D (H2 underwrites the stability claim for the tested regimes).

nodes.title: Synthetic subnetworks discovered by distilled pruning can be stable at initialization even when the dense initialization is unstable

nodes.content: Subnetworks produced by distilled pruning exhibit quantitatively and visually flatter loss landscapes than both the dense model and IMP-chosen subnetworks: (a) two-dimensional loss landscape visualizations around trained models on ConvNet-3 and CIFAR-10 show that synthetic subnetworks fall into a single, flat basin across different random seeds while the dense and IMP cases display separate minima separated by barriers; and (b) the diagonal of the empirical Hessian computed over training batches for ConvNet-3 on CIFAR-10 shows that synthetic subnetworks have a distribution of diagonal Hessian entries concentrated closer to zero with smaller variance and lower average magnitude than the dense model or IMP subnetworks at matched sparsities (sampled sparsities included 60% and 90% in the reported study).

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that synthetic subnetworks have flatter loss landscapes is supported by convergent evidence: Hessian diagonal statistics (H3) and loss landscape visualizations. However, the evidence is confined to a single architecture-dataset pair (ConvNet-3, CIFAR-10) and the Hessian measurements lack error bars across seeds (P3). P3 tempers the quantitative strength of the claim, narrowing its scope. The core insight is plausible and qualitatively robust for this setting, but the quantitative flattening measure may not be as precise as it appears. The interaction is cumulative: P3 only weakens, not invalidates, the quantitative pillar, while the qualitative pillar remains intact.

nodes.title: Distilled pruning selects parameters that yield flatter loss landscapes; synthetic subnetworks have tighter Hessian diagonal distributions and fall into the same flat basin across seeds

nodes.content: Applying Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with weight rewinding to a sparsity mask obtained by distilled pruning (starting IMP from a distilled-pruning-produced sparse initialization rather than the original dense initialization) yields sparse initializations that behave as true lottery tickets at substantially higher overall sparsities than IMP applied to the original dense initialization. Empirically, performing 8 distilled-pruning iterations (pruning 20% of weights per iteration to produce an intermediate stable mask at 83% sparsity) and then running IMP (still rewinding to initialization) finds sparse initializations that match or exceed the performance of IMP with weight rewinding to the third training epoch and that reach higher sparsities than achievable by IMP from the dense initialization. On ImageNet-10 with ResNet-10, this hybrid method yields lottery tickets with up to an order of magnitude fewer parameters compared to IMP applied to the dense initialization.

metadata.narrative: The ability of the hybrid method to find lottery tickets at higher sparsities than vanilla IMP is demonstrated on ImageNet-10 with ResNet-10, including a strong comparison to early-rewinding baselines (H4). However, the demonstration uses a fixed intermediate sparsity (83% from 8 steps) and is limited to a small-scale dataset (P4). The conclusion's general applicability is uncertain; the method's success may depend on fine-tuning the intermediate sparsity and distillation quality, which are unexplored. H4 and P4 do not offset—H4 establishes a proof of concept, P4 questions its generality. The dominant risk (P4) narrows the conclusion's scope to a single experimental configuration.

nodes.title: Using distilled pruning to generate a stable sparse initialization enables traditional IMP to find lottery tickets at higher sparsities than IMP from the original dense initialization

nodes.content: When using trajectory-matching distilled datasets of appropriate quality for the target model (e.g., Efficient Dataset Condensation tuned for the target architecture), Distilled Pruning matches the test accuracy of traditional IMP on ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 while using roughly 150x fewer real training points to generate the sparsity mask (example distilled settings: 10 images per class). However, across a range of datasets and compression ratios, the performance of synthetic subnetworks relative to IMP depends strongly on the distilled-data accuracy: on more complex tasks or when distilled data under-performs (e.g., CIFAR-100 or larger datasets with poorer distilled accuracy), synthetic subnetworks tend to be more stable but can underperform IMP in final test accuracy. Thus, distilled pruning provides an empirical trade-off: substantial reductions in inner-loop data usage and increased stability, at the cost of relying on high-quality distilled data to preserve performance.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion is primarily a characterization of the trade-off between stability and performance when using distilled pruning. The systematic mapping across architectures, datasets, and compression ratios (H5) provides a strong empirical foundation for the trade-off description. The performance-matching claim (distilled pruning matches IMP on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10) is specific to the tested configuration; its generality is bounded by the data quality dependence already stated. No load-bearing weak points were identified that threaten the conclusion as scoped; the evidence is transparent about limitations. The highlight H5 underwrites the trade-off characterization layer.

nodes.title: Distilled pruning can match IMP performance on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 while using orders-of-magnitude fewer training points, but performance depends on distilled-data quality

nodes.content: Empirical analysis of the binary sparsity masks produced from the same random initialization shows that the locations of pruned parameters chosen by distilled pruning are nearly independent from those chosen by IMP: the distribution of zeros across layers does not reveal a consistent structural pattern that differentiates the two methods, and the magnitudes of weights that are pruned at initialization follow similar distributions between methods. In other words, distilled pruning and IMP select largely distinct sets of parameters to remove even when starting from the same initialization, despite producing different downstream stability and curvature properties.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that distilled pruning and IMP produce structurally uncorrelated sparsity masks with similar magnitude distributions is presented without quantitative support (P5). No specific measurement (overlap coefficient, distribution comparison) or statistical test is reported. The conclusion therefore lacks the empirical foundation needed to be credited. The mechanistic insight that would follow from the claim remains unestablished. There are no highlights to offset this weakness.

nodes.title: Sparsity masks produced by distilled pruning and by IMP are structurally uncorrelated while sharing similar per-weight magnitude distributions at initialization

nodes.content: The distilled pruning procedure—iterative magnitude pruning applied to a neural network by repeatedly training to convergence on a small synthetic dataset produced via trajectory-matching dataset distillation (e.g., Efficient Dataset Condensation with 10 images per class), then pruning 20% of weights by magnitude, then rewinding the remaining weights to their random initialization—rests on the assumption that the relative ordering of weight magnitudes after training on the synthetic dataset matches the ordering that would be obtained after training on the full real dataset. The trajectory-matching distillation may preserve the training path but does not guarantee that final weight magnitudes across different parameters rank importance in the same way as real-data training, especially for parameters that encode rare or outlier patterns that are compressed out of the synthetic set.

metadata.failure_mode: If the weight magnitude ordering diverges between synthetic and real training, the distilled pruning procedure may prune parameters that are actually important for real-data performance, leading to a subnetwork that cannot be trained to the claimed performance levels (e.g., matching IMP accuracy on CIFAR-10) or that degrades at higher sparsities. The central claim that the procedure "produces sparse subnetworks at initialization" that can be effectively trained is directly undermined because the masks would be suboptimal.
metadata.weakness_reason: The synthetic dataset compresses multiple real images into a few synthetic exemplars; while trajectory matching may produce a similar training trajectory in parameter space, the convergence point and weight magnitudes at that point depend on the exact data distribution. Parameters that specialize to patterns unique to specific real images may have small magnitudes under synthetic training because those patterns are absent or merged, leading to incorrect pruning decisions. Without a validation step (e.g., comparing weight magnitude orderings between synthetic and real training), this assumption remains unverified.

nodes.title: Assumption that synthetic training preserves weight magnitude ordering

nodes.content: The linear mode connectivity experiments that show synthetic subnetworks (produced by distilled pruning on trajectory-matching distilled data) are stable to SGD noise at initialization—exhibiting low loss barriers under weight interpolation between models trained with different data orderings—are conducted on only two small-scale settings: ConvNet-3 with CIFAR-10 and ResNet-10 with ImageNet-10 (a 10-class subset of ImageNet-1K). Therefore, it is unknown whether the stability property generalizes to larger architectures (e.g., ResNet-50, ResNet-101) or full-scale datasets (e.g., ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-21K).

metadata.failure_mode: If the stability does not generalize to larger-scale settings, the conclusion that "synthetic subnetworks discovered by distilled pruning can be stable at initialization even when the dense initialization is unstable" is still true for the tested small-scale settings, but its significance and practical utility are substantially reduced. The paper's broader implication—that distilled pruning extends lottery-ticket-style results to larger models—would fail because the enabling property (stability) would not hold outside the tested regime.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's experiments are limited to models with at most ~5 million parameters (ResNet-10) and datasets with at most 10 classes (CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10). Larger models and datasets have previously been shown to be more complex and less stable (Frankle et al., 2020). Without evidence that the stability phenomenon scales, the claim should be scoped to the tested regimes. The paper does not provide theoretical justification or empirical scaling laws.

nodes.title: Small-scale scope of stability experiments

nodes.content:
For the claim that synthetic subnetworks have flatter loss landscapes, the Hessian diagonal analysis is performed only on ConvNet-3 trained on CIFAR-10. The diagonal Hessian entries are computed over batches of real training data for models that were trained on synthetic data. The distribution statistics (mean, standard deviation, range) are reported without confidence intervals or error bars across seeds; the differences in mean between synthetic and IMP are small (e.g., mean values 0.0047 vs 0.0051 at 60% sparsity) while standard deviations are large (0.0286 vs 0.0559). This single architectural and dataset configuration, with limited statistical characterization, may not demonstrate a general quantitative flattening of the loss landscape.
      Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the Hessian differences are not statistically robust or do not generalize to other architectures/datasets, the quantitative component of the claim (tighter Hessian diagonal distributions) is weakened. The qualitative claim about flat basins (from visualization) may still stand, but the Hessian evidence is a key quantitative pillar that would lose support, making the overall conclusion less solid.
metadata.weakness_reason: The Hessian diagonal measurement is a proxy for curvature but is known to be noisy; the reported standard deviations are comparable to or larger than mean differences across methods, raising questions about statistical significance. Additionally, the measurement is on real data after training on synthetic data, which may introduce a distribution shift: the model's parameters are optimized for synthetic data, so curvature on real data may not reflect the model's natural loss landscape. Without multiple independent seeds or bootstrap estimates, the quantitative support for flatness is limited.

nodes.title: Limited Hessian evidence for flatness

nodes.content:
For the claim that applying traditional IMP to a distilled-pruning-produced stable sparse initialization yields lottery tickets at substantially higher sparsities than IMP from the original dense initialization, the experimental demonstration is performed only on ImageNet-10 with ResNet-10. The "stable sparse initialization" is produced by 8 steps of distilled pruning (20% per iteration to reach 83% sparsity). The number of distilled pruning steps (8) and the resulting 83% sparsity initialization are obtained by a fixed protocol; there is no analysis of how this choice affects downstream IMP performance or whether a different number of steps would be better. The general claim that the hybrid method extends lottery tickets to higher sparsities is therefore demonstrated only for one specific protocol on a small-scale dataset.
      Figure 7

metadata.failure_mode: If the hybrid method's success depends sensitively on the intermediate sparsity or the number of distilled pruning steps, and these are not robust to changes in dataset/architecture, then the conclusion that the method "enables traditional IMP to find lottery tickets at higher sparsities" may not hold for other settings. The paper's central demonstration on ImageNet-10 becomes a singular proof-of-concept rather than a general recipe.
metadata.weakness_reason: The choice of 8 pruning steps (83% sparsity) for the stable initialization is arbitrary and may be sensitive to the distillation quality, dataset, and architecture. The paper does not explore alternative intermediate sparsities or validate that the resulting stable mask is optimal for subsequent IMP. On larger datasets, the computational cost of 8 iterations (even on synthetic data) may be non-negligible, and the stability of the intermediate mask may degrade with poorer distillation quality. Without broader validation, the method's applicability and effectiveness beyond the specific testbed are uncertain.

nodes.title: Hybrid method evaluated only on small-scale dataset

nodes.content: The claim that sparsity masks produced by distilled pruning and by IMP are structurally uncorrelated (nearly independent distribution of zeros across layers) and that the magnitudes of pruned weights at initialization share the same distribution between methods is supported only by a qualitative observation that no noticeable structure or pattern was found. No quantitative evidence is provided: no Jaccard overlap coefficient, no correlation statistic, no distribution overlap metric (e.g., Kolmogorov–Smirnov test), and no visual comparison of magnitude distributions are reported.

metadata.failure_mode: If the structural independence claim is unsupported, the conclusion that masks are structurally uncorrelated is not established. This weakens the paper's proposed mechanistic narrative that distilled pruning removes different parameters, which in turn explains the different stability and curvature properties. The conclusion's contribution to understanding the mechanism is lost.
metadata.weakness_reason: Without quantitative metrics, the claim of structural independence is not empirically supported. A visual or informal inspection of binary masks cannot reliably distinguish between random independent masks and masks with weak structural correlation. The statement about magnitude distributions being similar is similarly unsupported. Acceptable evidence would include overlap fraction, Jaccard similarity per layer, or distribution plots with summary statistics.

nodes.title: No quantitative evidence for mask structure claims

nodes.content: The distilled pruning procedure is validated on ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 using a trajectory-matching distilled dataset with 10 images per class (150x compression). In this setting, the synthetic subnetworks achieve test accuracy within error bars of traditional IMP subnetworks across sparsities up to 80%, as shown in Figure 2 (left panel).

metadata.credit: This empirical validation provides evidence that the procedure can produce functional sparsity masks in a non-trivial setting (ResNet-18 is a standard architecture, CIFAR-10 is a standard benchmark). Without this result, the conclusion that distilled pruning "produces sparse subnetworks at initialization" would be an untested algorithmic proposal. The validation's specificity (matched sparsities, error bars across 4 seeds) demonstrates that the method is not merely conceptual but operational, and that the masks it produces support real-data training to competitive accuracy. This guards against the failure mode where the procedure fails to produce useful masks due to synthetic/real distribution shift.

nodes.title: Empirical validation of distilled pruning on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10

nodes.content: For ConvNet-3 on CIFAR-10, the linear mode connectivity experiments (Figure 3, left column) show that synthetic subnetworks across sparsities 0%, 60%, 87%, 96%, and 99% have loss barriers that decrease with sparsity, reaching near-zero at high sparsities, while IMP subnetworks (middle column) retain significant barriers. This pattern is replicated on a second architecture-dataset pair: ResNet-10 on ImageNet-10 (Figure 4). In both cases, the dense model is unstable; the synthetic subnetworks become stable.

metadata.credit: The cross-architecture and cross-dataset replication guards against the failure mode where the stability property is an artifact of a single experimental setup. It shows that the phenomenon is reproducible under different model sizes (ConvNet-3 vs ResNet-10) and data distributions (CIFAR-10 vs ImageNet-10). Without this replication, the conclusion would rest on a single data point, leaving the claim vulnerable to unobserved confounders (e.g., a peculiarity of CIFAR-10 and ConvNet-3). The systematic sweep across sparsities (5 levels) further strengthens the trend.

nodes.title: Cross-architecture replication of stability

nodes.content: For ConvNet-3 on CIFAR-10, the diagonal Hessian evaluation over real training batches (Table 1) shows that synthetic subnetworks at 60% and 90% sparsity have consistently smaller standard deviations (0.0286 and 0.0354) and narrower value ranges (-0.982 to 2.093 and -2.338 to 1.730) compared to the dense model (std 0.035, range -1.847 to 1.344) and IMP subnetworks at matched sparsities (std 0.0559 and 0.0594, ranges -3.073 to 4.510 and -6.323 to 6.127). The mean and average magnitude are also lower for synthetic at 90% sparsity.

metadata.credit: This quantitative measurement provides a direct, continuous-valued metric of curvature that complements the qualitative loss landscape visualization. It guards against the failure mode where the flatness observed in the 2D projection is an artifact of the projection method. The synthetic subnetworks' Hessian diagonals are indeed tighter (lower variance, narrower range) than dense and IMP baselines, providing a concrete numerical basis for the claim of flatter landscapes. Without this, the conclusion would rely solely on visual inspection.

nodes.title: Quantitative Hessian diagonal evidence for flatter landscapes

nodes.content: The experiment in Figure 7 compares three methods on ImageNet-10 with ResNet-10: traditional IMP from dense initialization (IMP k=0), IMP with early rewinding to epoch 3 (IMP k=3, which produces matching subnetworks but not lottery tickets), and traditional IMP applied to the synthetic subnetwork from 8 steps of distilled pruning (hybrid method). At densities below 0.15 (sparsities above 85%), IMP k=0 performance drops below 65% test accuracy while the hybrid method maintains performance above 70% at density 0.05 (95% sparsity), and matches the performance of IMP k=3 which is not a lottery ticket. The hybrid method retains the "from initialization" property of true lottery tickets.

metadata.credit: The inclusion of the early-rewinding baseline (IMP k=3) provides a meaningful reference point: it is the current state-of-the-art for yielding trainable sparse networks from unstable initializations. The hybrid method matches its performance while strictly being a lottery ticket (training from initialization). This guards against the failure mode where the hybrid method's advantage is merely against an ablated version of IMP (k=0) that is known to fail, without comparison to the best available alternative. The demonstration that the hybrid method recovers the from-initialization property is the key conceptual advance.

nodes.title: Direct comparison to early-rewinding baseline showing lottery ticket advantage

nodes.content: Figure 6 plots the performance ratio (synthetic subnetwork test accuracy divided by IMP subnetwork test accuracy) versus the loss barrier height ratio (synthetic barrier / IMP barrier) for multiple configurations: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ConvNet-3, ResNet-18, and AlexNet; compression ratios from 50x to 500x. The plot shows a clear partition: points to the left of IMP's reference ratio (less stable) and below 1 (worse performance) correspond to CIFAR-100 settings where distilled performance is low; points to the right (more stable) and above 1 (better performance) correspond to CIFAR-10/ResNet-18/10 ipc settings. This systematically maps the trade-off between stability and performance determined by distilled-data quality.

metadata.credit: The multi-configuration scatter plot provides a comprehensive characterization of when distilled pruning benefits (stable) versus harms (performance loss). Without this systematic mapping, the conclusion's caveat about data-quality dependence would be a plausible suspicion rather than a documented empirical regularity. The explicit quantification of the trade-off across multiple datasets, architectures, and compression levels guards against the failure mode where the trade-off is only observed in a single configuration, allowing a reader to judge applicability to their setting.

nodes.title: Systematic mapping of stability-performance trade-off across multiple configurations

steps.reasoning: Define Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) as the following procedure: train a model to convergence on a dataset, prune a fraction of weights with smallest absolute value (magnitude), rewind the remaining weights to an earlier point (in this work to the original random initialization), and repeat these steps until the desired global sparsity is reached; the output is a binary sparsity mask indicating which parameters remain active. Define "weight rewinding" as restoring non-pruned weights to their values at the chosen rewind point (here, the original random initialization). Define "sparsity mask" as a binary mask $M$ with entries $M_i\in\{0,1\}$ indicating whether parameter $i$ is retained ($1$) or pruned ($0$).

Define dataset distillation as the optimization of a small synthetic dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ so that training an algorithm $\Phi$ on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ yields similar performance on a validation set $\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}$ as training $\Phi$ on the real dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}$; formally, the distillation objective is to minimize the absolute difference in validation loss between training on real and synthetic data:
$\displaystyle \arg\min_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}}\left|L\big(\Phi(\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}});\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}\big)-L\big(\Phi(\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}});\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}\big)\right|$,
where $L(\theta;\mathcal{D})$ denotes the average loss of parameters $\theta$ on dataset $\mathcal{D}$ and $\Phi(\mathcal{D})$ denotes the parameters returned by the training procedure $\Phi$ when trained on dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Cite the trajectory-matching style of distillation used in this work. 
Cazenavette et al. (2022)

State the operational desideratum: replace the expensive inner-loop training on the full real dataset inside IMP with training on a small synthetic distilled dataset, while preserving the semantics of iterative pruning with weight rewinding so that the final binary mask $M$ can be applied to the original random initialization and yield a subnetwork trainable on the real data. This desideratum requires (a) a distilled dataset that approximates the converged minima of SGD on real data, and (b) an explicit rule for pruning and rewinding when the inner-loop training uses synthetic data instead of real data.

Specify the Distilled Pruning algorithm as implemented and described in the paper: (i) construct a synthetic distilled dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ using a trajectory-matching dataset distillation method (examples in this work use 1–50 images per class); (ii) initialize the network with random weights $\theta_0$ and set the current mask $M\leftarrow\mathbf{1}$ (all ones); (iii) iteratively repeat: train the current masked network (weights masked by $M$) to convergence on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ using the standard training algorithm $\Phi$, prune the lowest-magnitude $p$ fraction of weights (here $p=0.20$ per iteration) according to their magnitudes after training to update $M$ by setting the corresponding entries to $0$, rewind the remaining unpruned weights to their original initialization values $\theta_0$, and continue until the desired global sparsity is reached; (iv) output the final mask $M_{\text{syn}}$ and define the "synthetic subnetwork" as the parameter vector $\theta_0\odot M_{\text{syn}}$ where $\odot$ denotes elementwise multiplication.
Figure 1

Clarify how the resulting synthetic subnetwork is used: after obtaining the final mask $M_{\text{syn}}$, train the masked initialization $\theta_0\odot M_{\text{syn}}$ on the real dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}$ using the same training procedure $\Phi$ to obtain the final performance; this mirrors the usage of masks obtained by standard IMP but replaces the expensive inner-loop dataset with $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ during mask discovery.

Provide empirical cost and data-usage claims observed in the experiments: when $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ contains 10 images per class for CIFAR-10 (i.e., 10 images per class distilled dataset), Distilled Pruning generates masks while using orders of magnitude fewer real data points in the inner loop compared to standard IMP; the empirical plots comparing distilled pruning and traditional IMP on ResNet-18 & CIFAR-10 (with distilled set = 10 images per class) show that Distilled Pruning uses far fewer real-data training points to find a sparsity mask, as summarized in the right panel of the referenced performance figure.
Figure 2

Note practical parameter choices used in the paper's experiments, making the procedure concrete: the inner-loop training on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ is run to convergence per pruning iteration, pruning removes the lowest 20% by magnitude each iteration, the remaining weights are rewound to the original random initialization $\theta_0$, and distilled datasets of sizes in the range 1–50 images per class are used in reported experiments (these choices instantiate the algorithm described above and correspond to the empirical results in figures).
Figure 1

Record an explicit claim about what Distilled Pruning produces and how it is interpreted: the binary sparsity mask $M_{\text{syn}}$ produced by iterative pruning on distilled data applied to the original initialization $\theta_0$ defines a "synthetic subnetwork" which can be subsequently trained on the real dataset; this empirical protocol and interpretation is the operational content of "Distilled Pruning" introduced in the paper.

Treat Distilled Pruning and its output synthetic subnetwork mask $M_{\text{syn}}$ as established (result of conclusion 1): $M_{\text{syn}}$ is assumed known and is obtained by the iterative distilled-pruning procedure that trains on a distilled dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$, prunes by smallest-magnitude weights, and rewinds to initialization $\theta_0$.

Define linear mode connectivity (LMC) and "stability to SGD noise" as used in the experiments: two trained parameter vectors $\theta^{(a)}$ and $\theta^{(b)}$ are said to be linearly mode connected if the training loss evaluated along the linear interpolation path $\theta(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)\theta^{(a)}+\alpha\theta^{(b)}$ for $\alpha\in[0,1]$ does not exhibit an increase (barrier) above the losses at the endpoints; "stable to SGD noise" means that training from the same initialization under different data shufflings or random seeds yields models that are linearly mode connected.

Describe the experimental protocol used to assess stability for synthetic subnetworks: (i) sample a random initialization $\theta_0$, (ii) generate a sparsity mask either via Distilled Pruning ($M_{\text{syn}}$) or via standard IMP ($M_{\text{IMP}}$) on the same initialization, (iii) for a given mask $M$, train the masked initialization $\theta_0\odot M$ twice with two different shufflings/orders of the real training data to obtain two trained parameters $\theta^{(1)}$ and $\theta^{(2)}$, and (iv) compute the training loss at points $\theta(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)\theta^{(1)}+\alpha\theta^{(2)}$ for $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and record whether this interpolated loss exhibits a barrier (increase) relative to endpoint losses.

Report the empirical observations for studied model-dataset settings: in the reported experiments for ConvNet-3 on CIFAR-10 and for ResNet-10 on ImageNet-10, the dense initialization (i.e., training the full dense model from $\theta_0$ under different data shufflings) is unstable and produces trained models that are not linearly mode connected (the interpolated loss exhibits a barrier), yet the synthetic subnetworks obtained by pruning on distilled data ($M_{\text{syn}}$) exhibit low or zero loss barriers under linear interpolation between independently trained versions of the same masked initialization, indicating linear mode connectivity for the sparse initialization. These observations are summarized in the linear interpolation plots and comparisons across sparsities.

Figure 4

Interpret the empirical implication: because the interpolated training loss for synthetic subnetworks does not increase between independently trained instances (different data orderings), synthetic subnetworks are stable to SGD noise at initialization even when the corresponding dense initialization is unstable; thus, pruning using distilled data can produce sparse initializations that satisfy the stability condition associated with the existence of lottery tickets (trainable sparse subnetworks from initialization) despite instability of the unpruned dense model.

Record the authors' qualitative hypothesis about why distilled pruning yields this effect: distilled data suppresses image-specific outlier information and concentrates label information in a compressed set, and pruning on such compressed data tends to remove parameters that would otherwise capture outlier-dependent sharp directions, thereby producing masks that lead to flatter basins and linear mode connectivity across seeds. This is stated as a postulate grounded in the observed stability differences (no formal derivation is provided).

Treat Distilled Pruning and its empirical outputs as established (result of conclusion 1): synthetic subnetworks $M_{\text{syn}}$ exist and are obtained by pruning on distilled data. Also accept empirical stability of synthetic subnetworks in certain settings (result of conclusion 2) as background for the landscape and curvature analyses that follow.

Describe the two-dimensional loss landscape visualization method used in the paper: take two independently trained parameter vectors (from different random seeds or data shufflings) arising from training the same masked initialization; form two direction vectors from these trained parameters and orthogonalize them to obtain two basis vectors $v_1,v_2$ spanning a two-dimensional affine subspace in parameter space; sample a grid of 10,000 points in this 2-D plane where each sampled parameter is a linear combination $\theta(\alpha,\beta)=\theta_{\text{center}}+\alpha v_1+\beta v_2$ for $(\alpha,\beta)$ in the grid; for each sampled $\theta(\alpha,\beta)$ evaluate the training loss on the real training dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}$. This maps a local neighborhood of the high-dimensional loss surface to a two-dimensional landscape that can be visualized.

Report visualization results and interpretation: for ConvNet-3 on CIFAR-10, the two-dimensional loss landscapes around trained models reveal that synthetic subnetworks fall into a single, flat basin across different random seeds (the sampled 2-D loss surface shows a contiguous flat region without distinct separated minima), whereas the dense model and IMP-selected subnetworks display separate minima that are separated by loss barriers in the 2-D projection; this explains why interpolations in the synthetic case do not exhibit barriers while those in IMP and dense cases do. These visual comparisons are presented in the referenced loss landscape figures.

Define the empirical Hessian diagonal measurement used to quantify curvature: denote the loss function by $L(\theta;\mathcal{D})$ and the Hessian matrix by $H(\theta)=\nabla_{\theta}^2 L(\theta;\mathcal{D})$; because computing the full Hessian is computationally prohibitive, the authors compute only the diagonal entries of the empirical Hessian over batches of real training data, i.e., the set $\{H_{ii}(\theta)\}_{i}$ where $H_{ii}(\theta)$ denotes the second derivative of the loss with respect to parameter $\theta_i$ evaluated on a training batch (the authors state they compute the diagonal over batches to approximate curvature).

Present the quantitative Hessian-diagonal results for ConvNet-3 on CIFAR-10 as reported in the paper's table (reproducing the tabulated statistics): for each subnetwork type the authors report sparsity, min/max diagonal entry, mean $\pm$ standard deviation of diagonal entries, and average magnitude of diagonal entries.

- IMP (sparsity $60\%$): min/max $=-3.073/4.510$, mean $\pm$ std $=0.0051\pm0.0559$, average magnitude $=0.0087$.
- IMP (sparsity $90\%$): min/max $=-6.323/6.127$, mean $\pm$ std $=0.0035\pm0.0594$, average magnitude $=0.0060$.

- Synthetic (sparsity $90\%$): min/max $=-2.338/1.730$, mean $\pm$ std $=0.0037\pm0.0354$, average magnitude $=0.0053$.

Interpret the Hessian-diagonal statistics: compared to the dense model and IMP-selected subnetworks, synthetic subnetworks have a distribution of diagonal Hessian entries that is concentrated closer to zero, with smaller variance and generally lower average magnitude; e.g., the synthetic 60% case exhibits min/max values with smaller absolute extremes ($-0.982$ to $2.093$) and a smaller standard deviation ($0.0286$) than the IMP 60% case (min/max $-3.073$/$4.510$, std $0.0559$), indicating empirically flatter curvature for synthetic subnetworks.

Combine visualization and curvature findings to conclude mechanistic link: because synthetic subnetworks fall into a single, flat basin in 2-D landscape visualizations and exhibit tighter Hessian-diagonal statistics (closer to zero, smaller variance), the paper concludes that distilled pruning selects parameters that yield flatter loss landscapes; this flatness across seeds explains the observed linear mode connectivity (stability) of synthetic subnetworks.

Treat Distilled Pruning (conclusion 1) and the empirical stability of synthetic subnetworks (conclusion 2) as established premises: Distilled Pruning can produce a sparse initialization $\theta_0\odot M_{\text{syn}}$ that is empirically stable to SGD noise (linearly mode connected across seeds) in settings where the dense initialization is unstable.

State the hybrid strategy proposed and implemented: first perform a small number $k_{\text{syn}}$ of distilled-pruning iterations starting from the dense initialization to obtain an intermediate stable sparsity mask $M_{\text{syn},k_{\text{syn}}}$ (an example in the experiments uses $k_{\text{syn}}=8$ pruning iterations), then use this sparse initialization $\theta_0\odot M_{\text{syn},k_{\text{syn}}}$ as the starting point for traditional Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with weight rewinding to initialization (i.e., when running IMP the algorithm still rewinds to $\theta_0$ but now the optimization and pruning steps operate on an initial mask that is already sparse and stable).

Explain why this hybrid can enable finding lottery tickets at higher sparsities: because the distilled-pruning preprocessing produces a sparse initialization that is stable to SGD noise, subsequent IMP iterations that use post-training weight magnitudes to decide further pruning are less likely to be invalidated by retraining-induced jumps to different minima; hence, applying IMP on a stable sparse initialization allows the usual weight-rewinding IMP logic (prune based on trained magnitudes, rewind to initialization, repeat) to succeed at higher overall sparsities than when IMP begins from an unstable dense initialization.

Describe the empirical protocol used to validate the hybrid procedure: (i) starting from $\theta_0$, run Distilled Pruning for $k_{\text{syn}}$ iterations to obtain $M_{\text{syn},k_{\text{syn}}}$ (example: $k_{\text{syn}}=8$), (ii) apply IMP with weight rewinding to this sparse initialization while still rewinding to $\theta_0$ at each IMP iteration, and (iii) after completing IMP, train the final masked initialization on real data and record test accuracy versus global sparsity; compare these curves to vanilla IMP starting from the dense initialization (IMP $k=0$) and to IMP with rewinding to an early training epoch (IMP $k=3$, which the authors note is not a lottery ticket because it does not train from initialization).

Report the observed empirical outcomes and comparative claims: in the experiments (for example on ImageNet subsets and ResNet variants), vanilla IMP starting from the dense initialization cannot find lottery tickets past certain high sparsities (e.g., IMP $k=0$ unable to find lottery tickets beyond approximately 90% sparsity in the presented figure), whereas the hybrid approach that first performs a modest number (e.g., 8) of distilled-pruning iterations to obtain a stable sparse initialization and then applies IMP on that initialization finds sparse initializations that match or exceed the performance of IMP with early rewinding and reach higher sparsities than vanilla IMP; the paper reports finding lottery tickets with significantly fewer parameters on ImageNet subsets (stated as up to an order-of-magnitude fewer parameters in the experiments) when using the distilled-pruning + IMP hybrid.
Figure 7

Explain the practical computation-cost perspective given by the authors: the small number of distilled-pruning iterations used to produce the stable intermediate mask (e.g., 8 iterations) incurs negligible compute compared to the cost of a full training run; therefore, the hybrid approach provides a computationally efficient preprocessing step that extends the reach of traditional IMP (with rewinding to initialization) to sparser regimes without resorting to rewinding-to-early-training strategies that violate the "from-initialization" lottery ticket requirement.

Restate the claim in methodological terms: using distilled pruning to generate a stable sparse initialization enables traditional IMP (which still rewinds to the original initialization) to discover true lottery-ticket-style sparse initializations at substantially higher sparsities than IMP applied directly to the original dense initialization, thereby extending the practical set of initializations that yield trainable sparse subnetworks from initialization.

Treat Distilled Pruning as defined and implemented (conclusion 1) as the starting point: Distilled Pruning obtains masks by training on small distilled datasets $\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}$ (e.g., 10 images per class) and pruning with weight rewinding to initialization.

Define the empirical performance comparison metric used in the experiments: for a target model and dataset, measure test accuracy of the sparse subnetwork obtained by Distilled Pruning when trained on real data, and compare it to the test accuracy of a subnetwork obtained by standard IMP under the same rewind-to-initialization protocol; additionally, quantify the amount of real training data used during mask discovery (e.g., number of real images seen by the inner-loop training across pruning iterations) and report the reduction relative to standard IMP.

Describe the distilled data method and its reported distilled-data accuracy characteristics relevant to the claim: the paper uses a trajectory-matching distillation method labeled Efficient Dataset Condensation (EDC) tuned for the target architecture; EDC obtains distilled-data test accuracies on CIFAR-10 in the range 50.6%–74.5% depending on distilled dataset size (1, 10, or 50 images per class), demonstrating that distilled-data quality varies with compression and model-specific tuning.
Kim et al. (2022)

Report the primary empirical result on ResNet-18 and CIFAR-10: when using trajectory-matching distilled datasets of appropriate quality (example: EDC with 10 images per class), Distilled Pruning matches the test accuracy of traditional IMP on ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 while using roughly 150x fewer real training points to generate the sparsity mask; this equivalence in test accuracy together with the dramatically reduced inner-loop real-data usage is illustrated in the comparative performance plots.
Figure 2

Explain how the reduction in real-data usage is quantified and give an illustrative compression calculation: define compression ratio as original dataset size divided by distilled dataset size; for CIFAR-10 with 5,000 training points per class distilled to 10 images per class, the compression ratio is $500$; the paper reports empirical reductions in the number of real training points used for mask discovery on the order of $10^2$ (e.g., approximately $150\times$ in reported ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 experiments), as shown in the right panel of the performance comparison figure that measures real-data consumption per method.
Figure 2

Report the dependence of final sparse-model performance on distilled-data quality and dataset complexity: across a range of datasets and compression ratios, the synthetic-subnetwork performance relative to IMP depends strongly on distilled-data accuracy; on more complex tasks (for example CIFAR-100) or when the distilled data has lower accuracy, synthetic subnetworks typically exhibit greater stability but can underperform IMP in final test accuracy. This trade-off—substantial reductions in inner-loop data usage and increased stability versus reliance on high-quality distilled data to preserve test performance—is empirically characterized in cross-dataset plots of performance ratio and loss-barrier ratio.
Figure 6

State the empirical conclusion drawn: Distilled Pruning can match IMP performance on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 while using orders-of-magnitude fewer training points when the distilled dataset is of adequate quality for the target model, but in general performance depends strongly on distilled-data quality and dataset complexity, yielding a trade-off between data-efficiency/stability and final accuracy.

Treat Distilled Pruning and standard IMP mask outputs as given (conclusion 1): starting from the same random initialization $\theta_0$, produce two binary masks $M_{\text{syn}}$ (from distilled pruning) and $M_{\text{IMP}}$ (from traditional IMP).

Describe the mask-comparison analysis performed by the authors: compare the binary masks entrywise to measure overlap (i.e., fraction of parameters where both masks retain or both prune the same parameter), examine per-layer sparsity patterns (the fraction of zeros per layer), and compare the distributions of absolute weight magnitudes at initialization for weights that are pruned by each method; these empirical diagnostics test whether the two methods select similar parameter locations or different ones and whether they prune weights with similar initial magnitudes.

Report the empirical findings as stated in the paper: the locations of pruned parameters chosen by distilled pruning are nearly independent from those chosen by IMP when both start from the same initialization — the masks do not exhibit a consistent structural pattern of overlap across layers, and the per-layer fractions of pruned weights are similar on aggregate but the specific indices pruned are largely distinct; additionally, the magnitudes of weights that are pruned at initialization follow similar distributions between the two methods, i.e., the per-weight magnitude histograms for pruned parameters look similar across distilled-pruning and IMP choices.

Interpret the implication: because distilled pruning and IMP remove largely distinct sets of parameters even though their per-weight magnitude statistics at initialization are similar, the differences in downstream stability and curvature properties (e.g., synthetic subnetworks being flatter and more stable) cannot be explained solely by reordering of a common set of pruned weights; instead, distilled pruning selects a different structural subset of parameters whose removal leads to altered landscape and stability properties.

Record the authors' admission of empirical limitations: the authors note that analyzing sparsity masks in isolation did not reveal clear structural patterns explaining the differences (no microcharacteristic such as feature selectivity or connectivity was identified), and they invite further analyses to determine which microcharacteristics govern selection differences between distilled pruning and IMP.

open_questions.content: Several scientifically meaningful limitations and directions remain unresolved. First, dataset distillation quality and generalization constrain distilled pruning: current distilled datasets under-perform on harder datasets and do not generalize well across architectures, so distilled pruning cannot yet serve as a standalone replacement for IMP when final test performance is the priority. Second, the mechanistic origin of why distilled pruning removes parameters that correlate with landscape sharpness remains incompletely characterized; although loss-landscape visualizations and Hessian diagonal statistics indicate reduced sharpness, a deeper theoretical understanding or layer-wise analytical account is not provided. Third, the absence of clear structural patterns in sparsity masks invites further analysis: it is an open empirical question which microcharacteristics of pruned parameters (e.g., their functional role, connectivity, or feature selectivity) determine whether distilled pruning or IMP will select them. Fourth, scaling distilled pruning to large datasets and architectures (e.g., full ImageNet-1K and large-scale vision or language models) requires improved distillation algorithms or alternative synthetic-data construction strategies (the authors suggest knowledge-distillation-from-dense-model approaches as a potential avenue), and it remains unresolved whether such advances can enable distilled pruning to find stable lottery tickets in real-world large-scale settings. Finally, the trade-off between increased stability and occasional loss in final accuracy when using distilled pruning is not yet algorithmically resolved: methods that preserve both high distilled-data compression and high downstream accuracy are an open research objective.
